summary:
Bahia, in Brazil's north-east, records trans and travesti killings at a rate that places it among the country's highest-burden states. The ANTRA 2025 dossier, reported by SBT News on 26 January 2026, counts 7 trans people killed in Bahia during 2025, behind only a handful of states; on the same reckoning Bahia ranks third nationally across 2017 to 2025 with 97 killings, after São Paulo (151) and Ceará (107). Valor Internacional reported the same state-level counts on 27 January 2026, and the figure appears in consecutive annual dossiers rather than in a single outlier year: the ANTRA dossier for 2022 ranked Bahia seventh among the states, with 7 killings of travestis recorded in the state that year.

The victim profile is consistent. The overwhelming majority of those killed are travestis and trans women, most aged 18 to 29, around 70% Black among cases in which race was identified, and most killings take place outside the state capital. The burden falls on Black trans women and on young people in interior municipalities, not on visitors to Salvador's tourist districts as a matter of statistical fact.

A specific case in December 2025 illustrates both the killing pattern and the response. G1 Bahia reported on 9 December 2025 that police were investigating the death of Rhianna, an 18-year-old trans woman, as a feminicide: she was strangled in Luís Eduardo Magalhães in the interior of Bahia on the weekend of 6–7 December. The suspect, a 19-year-old app driver, drove her body to the police station himself and was released after confessing and claiming self-defence; the Civil Police confirmed the feminicide classification notwithstanding the suspect's initial release.

Bahia-specific statutory restriction was not identified in the sources reviewed. The national framework governs: Brazil's Supreme Federal Tribunal ruled in 2019 that discrimination and hate crimes on sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds are criminal, with transphobia punishable on the same footing as racism, and same-sex couples' marriage and spousal-visa rights have operated nationwide since 2013. Nothing in the audited sources indicates a Bahia ordinance narrowing or widening those national rules.
tangentialFactors:
Bahia's position in the national count is driven partly by population size, but the relative standing is stable across the 2022 and 2025 dossiers: seventh on the 2022 tally, third on the 2017–2025 cumulative tally, and among the highest single-year counts in 2025. Ceará leads the cumulative ranking alongside São Paulo; Minas Gerais appears in the 2025 pair reported by Valor Internacional behind the leaders. The comparison shows a country-wide pattern with Bahia as one of the several worst-affected states, not an isolated local pathology.

The feminicide framing of the Rhianna case connects to a broader national movement: case-law analysis from 2022 records lower courts pressing the Superior Court of Justice toward extending the Maria da Penha Law and the Feminicide Law to trans women. Bahia's Civil Police applying a feminicide classification to a trans victim in 2025 sits within that trend rather than outside it, although the suspect's release after a self-defence claim shows the classification does not guarantee pre-trial detention.

The 2022 dossier also recapped emblematic Bahia cases and noted that Pernambuco led the national negative ranking that year, indicating that the state's share shifts year to year without the underlying pattern changing.
localsOnly:
Trans and travesti residents of Bahia face a documented and recurring risk of lethal violence, concentrated among young Black trans women in interior municipalities. The state has appeared in the top-ranked band of the national dossiers for consecutive years: seventh with 7 killings in 2022, and 97 recorded killings between 2017 and 2025.

Residents in detention are covered by the national framework, which applies in Bahia without state variation in the sources reviewed. LGBTQ prisoners are entitled to a designated place in Brazilian prisons, to be addressed by their social name rather than their birth name, to placement corresponding to their gender identity, and to choose male or female clothing. Same-sex partners have had the right to conjugal visits in all Brazilian jails since February 2015, under the National Criminal and Penitentiary Council.

The federal detention regime requires that placement decisions for LGBTI detainees be made by a judge in a reasoned decision after consulting the person's stated preference, prohibits the use of LGBTI-specific units as disciplinary isolation, and bans compulsory transfer as punishment.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Bahia-specific prison placement rule, special unit designation, or documented segregation practice was found. One source addressing LGBTQ prisoners in Brazilian jails contains a mention of Bahia that concerns a Salvador City Council candidate and carries no detention-housing content; the national prison framework is therefore reported without state-level correction or confirmation from Bahia's penitentiary administration.

Whether the 2025 count of 7 killings is an undercount is unresolved. National tallies of trans killings in Brazil are compiled by civil-society monitoring from press and family reports, and unreported cases cannot be ruled out from the available sources.

The sources do not state whether the feminicide investigation of Rhianna's killing has produced an arrest, charges, or a judicial order since December 2025. The suspect's release after confessing and claiming self-defence is documented, and the subsequent procedural history is not.
